summary: This informational document lists requirements for taking down or bringing up a BGP session gracefully. Simply dropping a session can cause traffic loss for customers even when backup paths exist. The requirements describe what a solution must do so operators can do maintenance with minimal disruption.

plainLanguage.summary: Closing a bridge for repairs without warning stops cars mid-trip. This document says what is needed so BGP routers can warn others first and traffic takes the detour smoothly.

questions: how to gracefully shut down a bgp session
how to avoid traffic loss during maintenance
subtitle: How routers can shut down BGP connections for maintenance without losing customer traffic.

tldr.problem: When a BGP session is shut down for maintenance, the router withdraws routes immediately, causing traffic loss even when alternate paths exist. This disrupts customer service during planned maintenance operations.
tldr.mechanism: A graceful shutdown mechanism warns BGP peers in advance of a session shutdown so they can converge on alternate paths before the session is actually terminated. Similarly, when a session is brought back up, peers are notified so they can switch back to the preferred path without traffic loss.
tldr.outcome: Operators can perform planned maintenance on BGP sessions and routers with minimal or zero traffic disruption, since traffic is rerouted before the session is closed and restored before the session is brought up.

today: RFC 6198 is an Informational RFC expressing requirements for graceful BGP shutdown mechanisms. It has not been obsoleted. Implementations addressing these requirements have been developed by router vendors and are deployed in service provider networks.

sections.title: The Maintenance Problem
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the core routing protocol for the Internet and is heavily used in service provider networks for both Internet routes and BGP/MPLS VPN services. Service providers maintain redundant routers and BGP sessions for resilience. However, when a BGP session is shut down for maintenance, BGP behaves as if there were a sudden link or router failure: it withdraws the prefixes learned over that session, triggering routing convergence and often causing traffic loss.

This happens even when an alternate path is available. Consider a customer dual-attached to two routers (ASBR1 and ASBR2). When ASBR1 shuts down its BGP session with the route reflector, it immediately withdraws routes. Traffic can be lost during the convergence period while routers search for and select alternate paths. This is unacceptable for modern applications like voice over IP and online gaming, which require minimal disruption during maintenance.

Unlike graceful restart (which applies when forwarding is preserved during control plane restart), graceful shutdown applies when forwarding is intentionally interrupted for maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, shutting down a router for maintenance is like suddenly closing a road without warning. Cars heading that way crash and have to find new routes on the fly, causing delays.

sections.title: Why Traffic Gets Lost
sections.content:
Two main causes of packet loss occur during maintenance: lack of an alternate path on some routers, and transient routing inconsistency.

Some routers may not know about the alternate path because a route reflector is only advertising its best path, or because the backup router prefers the nominal path over the backup and is not advertising the backup path. This lack of knowledge prevents those routers from rerouting traffic before the primary session shuts down.

Transient routing inconsistencies happen because routers do not simultaneously update their Routing Information Bases (RIBs) and Forwarding Information Bases (FIBs). During IBGP convergence, especially with hierarchical route reflectors, some routers may update before others. This creates temporary routing loops, which increase link congestion and cause packet drops.
sections.plainLanguage: Two problems happen: some routers do not know about a detour route, and routers update at different times creating temporary confusion about where traffic should go.

sections.title: Requirements for Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
The goal is to minimize traffic loss during planned shutdown and bring-up of BGP sessions. Ideally, loss is reduced to zero. A graceful shutdown solution should use a make-before-break approach: signal the upcoming shutdown in advance, allowing affected routers to converge on alternate paths and install them in their Forwarding Information Bases before the nominal session is shut down. All affected routers then have a valid path at every moment.

The solution must allow BGP routers to advertise that a session will soon be unavailable, ensuring that the old path is not removed from routing tables before a new path is known. The mechanism should apply to all BGP session types: EBGP, IBGP, route reflector client, confederations, and multiprotocol extensions, and to various network topologies. Incremental deployment must be possible, so that a solution can benefit networks even if not all routers are upgraded.

The solution should also minimize forwarding loops and apply to redistribution of static IP routes into BGP. The specific graceful shutdown procedure should end when the BGP session is closed and the nominal routing is restored, with discussion of how operators know when it is safe to complete the shutdown.
sections.plainLanguage: What the solution must do: warn first, let everyone find the detour, then close the road, then reopen it, and let everyone come back. Even if some routers are not upgraded, it should still help.

sections.title: Topologies That Must Be Supported
sections.content:
Graceful shutdown must work across a variety of BGP topologies. For External BGP (EBGP), it must support one-to-two redundancy (one router in AS1 connecting to two in AS2), two-to-two redundancy (symmetric protection in both directions), and multi-homed topologies (multiple interconnects to different ASes).

For Internal BGP (IBGP), it must support full-mesh topologies (every router peers with every other), route reflector topologies with one or multiple levels, and confederations (groups of ASes acting as one for certain purposes). For routing decisions, it must handle hot potato routing (based on IGP cost to reach the BGP next-hop), cold potato routing (based on BGP LOCAL_PREF set by the exit point or configured locally), and other policies.

A key consideration: unlike VPLS with distributed PEs, VPWS has no distributed PE model. If a PSN involves multiple operator domains (Multi-segment PW), graceful shutdown OAM domains remain unchanged since switched PEs are typically not aware of native service.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution must work whether there are two backup paths, ten backup paths, many route reflectors deciding paths, or different ways of choosing which path is best.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
At the requirements stage, graceful shutdown is not expected to create new security vulnerabilities because BGP neighbors already have the ability to send incorrect or misleading information. However, security solutions must address the risk of bogus g-shut messages that could disrupt routing. A solution must prevent an attacker from using fake graceful shutdown messages to manipulate routing decisions.

A solution should not increase the ability of one AS to selectively influence routing decisions in a peer AS beyond what is already possible. If such behavior is detected, the peer AS should have means to identify and react to it.

These security considerations will be addressed in more detail by solutions that implement the graceful shutdown mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors trust each other already. But solutions must prevent fake shutdown messages and block any new way to secretly change routes.
